questions.prompt: A chunk of granite is speckled with pink, white, gray and black grains. What are those different grains?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A chunk of granite is speckled with grains of four colors: pink, white, gray and black. What are those different grains?

choices.text: Different minerals, each with its own atom pattern
choices.rationale: Correct. Granite is a mix of several minerals, such as quartz, feldspars and mica. Each has its own chemical makeup and crystal pattern, and different minerals tend to show different colors.

choices.text: Bits of a single mineral stained by soil and rainwater
choices.rationale: Staining only tints a surface. These grains differ all the way through because they are different substances with different arrangements of atoms.

choices.text: Sand grains of different colors cemented together
choices.rationale: Cemented sand makes sandstone. Granite's grains are crystals that grew interlocked as magma cooled, with no cement between them.

choices.text: Tiny separate rocks melted together by lava
choices.rationale: The grains are minerals, the building blocks of rock. Granite's crystals grew side by side as magma cooled slowly underground, not from lava gluing rocks together.

questions.explanation: Most rocks are built from minerals, and minerals are built from crystals: atoms of one or more elements stacked in a repeating pattern. A typical granite holds four main minerals (quartz, biotite mica, and two feldspars, orthoclase and plagioclase), so its grains come in several colors.
questions.misconception: The colored grains in a rock are just stains, or bits of other rock stuck together.
questions.hint: Think about the building blocks one step smaller than the rock itself.

questions.prompt: Which statements about minerals are accurate? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Here are four statements about minerals. Choose every statement that is accurate. Select all that apply.

choices.text: A mineral's atoms are arranged in a repeating pattern.
choices.rationale: Correct. That orderly, repeating arrangement is what makes a mineral crystalline and gives it its shape.

choices.text: Each mineral has its own specific chemical makeup.
choices.rationale: Correct. Quartz is always silicon and oxygen, and halite is always sodium and chlorine, in fixed proportions. Some minerals, such as plagioclase feldspar, can vary within set limits, holding more sodium or more calcium.

choices.text: Most minerals are made of a single chemical element.
choices.rationale: Only a few minerals, such as diamond (pure carbon), are single elements. Most are compounds, like quartz (silicon and oxygen) and halite (sodium and chlorine).

choices.text: Volcanic glass is a mineral, since it is a natural solid.
choices.rationale: Natural glass is solid, but its atoms are jumbled instead of repeating in a pattern. With no crystal structure, it is not a mineral. That is why pumice, which is mostly glass, is not built mainly from minerals.

questions.explanation: A mineral forms naturally, has a definite chemical makeup, and has its atoms arranged in an orderly, repeating pattern, which shapes its crystals. Most minerals are compounds of two or more elements, such as quartz (silicon and oxygen). Natural glass is not a mineral, because its atoms do not repeat in a pattern.
questions.misconception: Minerals are pure elements, and any natural solid counts as a mineral.
questions.hint: Test each statement on two examples: quartz, and the natural glass in pumice.

questions.prompt: Sort each rock-making story into the type of rock it produces.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort seven rock-making stories into three rock types: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. The stories are: salt crystals remain as seawater dries up; lava spills from a volcano and hardens; limestone beside hot magma recrystallizes into marble; sand grains pile up in layers and get cemented; solid rock squeezed between colliding plates forms bands; magma cools for ages deep inside a mountain; and seashells pile up on the seafloor and harden.

items.text: Lava spills from a volcano and hardens
items.rationale: Igneous: molten rock that cools and hardens makes igneous rock, here quickly at the surface.

items.text: Magma cools for ages deep inside a mountain
items.rationale: Igneous: slow underground cooling of melted rock is how granite forms.

items.text: Sand grains pile up in layers and get cemented
items.rationale: Sedimentary: deposited rock fragments that are compacted and cemented make rock like sandstone.

items.text: Salt crystals remain as seawater dries up
items.rationale: Sedimentary: dissolved minerals crystallize out of the water and build up as halite (rock salt).

items.text: Seashells pile up on the seafloor and harden
items.rationale: Sedimentary: the remains of living things that settle in layers form rock such as limestone.

items.text: Limestone beside hot magma recrystallizes into marble
items.rationale: Metamorphic: heat changes an existing solid rock's crystals without melting it. The magma nearby is a heat source, not the rock that forms.

items.text: Solid rock squeezed between colliding plates forms bands
items.rationale: Metamorphic: pressure and heat reshape solid rock, lining up its crystals in bands.

questions.explanation: The rock type depends on how the rock formed. Melted rock that cools becomes igneous. Pieces of older rock or the remains of living things that settle and harden, and minerals that crystallize out of water, become sedimentary. Solid rock that heat and pressure change becomes metamorphic.
questions.misconception: Rock type depends on where a rock is found or how it looks, not on how it formed.
questions.hint: Ask of each story: did it start as melted rock, as settling bits, or as solid rock that got changed?

questions.prompt: Sand from a crumbling desert rock tower gets buried and squeezed under more sand. Over time, minerals carried by groundwater crystallize between the grains and cement them together, with no strong heating. What kind of rock forms?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sand from a crumbling desert rock tower gets buried and squeezed under more sand. Over time, minerals carried by groundwater crystallize between the grains and cement them together, and the sand is never strongly heated. What kind of rock forms?

choices.text: Sedimentary rock, since it is glued-together grains
choices.rationale: Correct. Compacted, cemented sand grains make sandstone, a sedimentary rock.

choices.text: Metamorphic rock, since burial squeezes it
choices.rationale: Burial pressure does pack the grains, but that compaction is part of making sedimentary rock. Metamorphism needs much more heat and pressure, enough to rebuild the crystals.

choices.text: Igneous rock, since new crystals grew between the grains
choices.rationale: The cement crystals did grow, but from minerals dissolved in groundwater, not from melted rock. Igneous rock forms only when melted rock cools.

choices.text: Not rock yet, since grains need heat to harden into rock
choices.rationale: Minerals carried by groundwater can glue grains into solid rock without any heating. That is how sandstone forms.

questions.explanation: Weathered grains that are carried, dropped, buried and cemented form sedimentary rock. The weight of overlying sand presses the grains together, and minerals left by groundwater crystallize between them and glue them. Those cement crystals grow from water, not from melted rock, and shallow burial is far from the intense heat and pressure of metamorphism.
questions.misconception: Squeezing or new crystal growth during burial turns sediment into metamorphic or igneous rock.
questions.hint: Squeezing and new crystals both show up in this story. Which one actually joined the grains, and what did those crystals grow from?

evidence.locator: Section 4. Sedimentary Processes, Physical Sedimentation and Figure 4A
evidence.supports: Physical weathering breaks rock into sediment; wind or water carries it and deposits it when it lacks the energy to keep it moving; breccia (large angular pebbles) and sandstone (small grains, compacted and cemented in layers) form this way.

evidence.locator: Section 6. Recycling the Three Types of Rock (Rock Castle)
evidence.supports: The Rock Castle is slowly breaking down into sand, and that sand will at some point be recycled into another rock formation.

evidence.title: Sedimentary Rocks
evidence.supports: If sediment is buried deeply it becomes compacted and cemented, forming sedimentary rock; cementation deposits minerals in the spaces between grains.

questions.prompt: Match each texture clue to the history it most likely points to.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Match each of four texture clues to the history it most likely points to. Histories: grains were carried and dropped by wind or water; solid rock was squeezed and heated deep underground; melted rock cooled quickly at the surface; melted rock cooled slowly underground.

left.text: Large crystals you can see without a lens
left.rationale: Slow cooling underground gives crystals a long time to grow, as in granite.

left.text: Crystals too small to see without a lens
left.rationale: Quick cooling at the surface stops crystals while they are still small, as in basalt.

left.text: Small sand grains in flat layers
left.rationale: Wind or water dropped the grains, layer on layer, as in sandstone.

left.text: Flattened crystals lined up in wavy bands
left.rationale: Squeezing and heat deformed solid rock, stretching and aligning its crystals, as in gneiss.

right.text: Melted rock cooled quickly at the surface
Grains were carried and dropped by wind or water
Solid rock was squeezed and heated deep underground

questions.explanation: Texture is a record of how a rock formed. Crystal size tells how fast melted rock cooled, layered grains tell of settling sediment, and lined-up crystals in bands tell of solid rock being squeezed. Reading texture is one of the first things geologists do with a new rock.
questions.misconception: A rock's texture is random and says nothing about how it formed.
questions.hint: Ask what process could make each pattern: growing crystals, settling grains, or squeezing.

questions.prompt: Two igneous rocks contain the same minerals in about the same amounts. One has crystals as big as peas; the other's crystals are too small to see. What best explains the difference?

choices.text: Their molten rock cooled at different speeds
choices.rationale: Correct. Same ingredients, different cooling time: slow cooling grows big crystals and fast cooling leaves tiny ones.

choices.text: The pea-crystal rock has heavier elements
choices.rationale: Both rocks have the same minerals, so their composition matches. Here crystal size comes from cooling time, not from which elements are present.

choices.text: The tiny crystals are still growing in the rock
choices.rationale: Once the rock is solid, its crystals stop growing. Small crystals mean growth was cut short by fast cooling.

choices.text: Pressure crushed the big crystals into small ones
choices.rationale: Crushing would leave broken fragments, not neat tiny crystals, and nothing suggests one rock was crushed.

questions.explanation: When magma cools, crystals start small and grow for as long as the rock stays molten. Slow cooling, such as deep underground, gives crystals time to grow large. Quick cooling, such as in lava at the surface, freezes them while they are still tiny.
questions.misconception: Crystal size in igneous rock is set by which elements the rock contains.
questions.hint: The ingredients are the same. What else could differ between the two batches of molten rock?

questions.prompt: Did each rock form from magma that hardened underground (intrusive) or from molten rock that cooled at the surface (extrusive)? Sort them.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort five rocks by where their molten rock cooled: underground, which is intrusive, or at the surface, which is extrusive. The rocks are: basalt from an ancient lava flow, now buried under younger rock layers; granite with large crystals found deep in a mine; glassy, bubble-filled pumice washed up on a beach; Enchanted Rock's granite dome, now exposed at the surface; and coarse-grained gabbro.

items.text: Granite with large crystals, found deep in a mine
items.rationale: Intrusive: large crystals mean slow cooling underground.

items.text: Enchanted Rock's granite dome, now exposed at the surface
items.rationale: Intrusive: its large crystals show it cooled slowly underground. Uplift and erosion exposed it later, so where it is now is not where it formed.

items.text: Coarse-grained gabbro
items.rationale: Intrusive: coarse grains mean the magma cooled slowly below the surface.

items.text: Basalt from an ancient lava flow, now buried under younger rock layers
items.rationale: Extrusive: it formed from lava that cooled quickly at the surface, keeping its crystals tiny. Younger layers buried it later, so where it sits now is not where it cooled.

items.text: Glassy, bubble-filled pumice washed up on a beach
items.rationale: Extrusive: its glassy, bubbly texture shows it cooled almost instantly after an eruption, so its melt froze as glass. Where it washed up does not change where it cooled.

questions.explanation: Texture tells where cooling happened: large crystals mean slow cooling underground, and tiny crystals or glass mean fast cooling at the surface. Location can fool you in both directions. Enchanted Rock cooled underground and was later lifted up and uncovered by erosion, while an old lava flow can end up buried under younger rock.
questions.misconception: Where an igneous rock is found today shows where it cooled.

questions.prompt: Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals. Chemical weathering changes or dissolves the minerals themselves. Sort each change.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort six changes into two groups: physical weathering, which breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals, and chemical weathering, which changes or dissolves the minerals themselves. The changes are: water freezes in a crack and wedges the rock apart; rainwater seeps into limestone and slowly hollows out a cave; iron-bearing minerals react with air and water and crumble into rust-colored grains; wind-blown sand scours grains off a cliff; a boulder splits after years of hot days and cold nights; and acids from decaying leaves and fungi slowly eat away a rock's minerals.

items.text: Water freezes in a crack and wedges the rock apart
items.rationale: Physical: ice takes up more space than water, so it pries the crack wider. The broken pieces are made of the same minerals as before.

items.text: Rainwater seeps into limestone and slowly hollows out a cave
items.rationale: Chemical: slightly acidic rainwater reacts with the limestone's calcite and carries it away dissolved.

items.text: Iron-bearing minerals react with air and water and crumble into rust-colored grains
items.rationale: Chemical: iron joins with oxygen to form rust, a new substance, which weakens the rock.

items.text: Wind-blown sand scours grains off a cliff
items.rationale: Physical: flying sand knocks bits off the rock, like sandpaper. The bits are still the same minerals.

items.text: A boulder splits after years of hot days and cold nights
items.rationale: Physical: the rock swells as it heats and shrinks as it cools, again and again, until it cracks.

items.text: Acids from decaying leaves and fungi slowly eat away a rock's minerals
items.rationale: Chemical: the acids react with the minerals and dissolve them.

questions.explanation: Physical weathering only breaks rock into smaller pieces, so the minerals stay the same; ice in cracks, wind-blown sand and big temperature swings all work this way. Chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves: water dissolves limestone, iron-bearing minerals rust, and acids from living things eat into rock. Both kinds turn solid rock into sediment.
questions.misconception: Any weathering that involves water must be chemical.
questions.hint: After each change, are the rock's minerals still the same stuff, just in smaller pieces?

evidence.locator: Section 4. Sedimentary Processes, Physical Sedimentation
evidence.supports: Temperature changes, wind, flowing water and gravity break rock into small fragments; this breakdown by physical processes is physical weathering.

evidence.locator: Section 4. Sedimentary Processes, Chemical Sedimentation
evidence.supports: Rock reacts chemically with air, water, soil and organisms and breaks down (chemical weathering); in dissolution, water breaks solid rock material down into dissolved material too small to see.

evidence.title: Weathering
evidence.supports: Mechanical (physical) weathering makes rock crumble, for example by frost wedging and by rock expanding with heat and contracting with cold; chemical weathering changes the molecular structure of rock, for example carbonic acid hollowing out caves in limestone, iron rusting with oxygen and water, and carbonic acid from decaying plants and fungi weakening and dissolving rock.

questions.limitations: Real rock often weathers both ways at once; each change is sorted by the process it describes.

questions.prompt: A fast, muddy river carrying sand and fine mud flows into a calm lake. Where does most of its sand settle, and why?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A fast-flowing, muddy river carries sand and fine mud into a calm lake. Where does most of the river's sand settle, and why?

choices.text: Near the river mouth, since the slowing water drops it
choices.rationale: Correct. Entering the calm lake, the river slows and loses the energy to carry sand, so the heavier sand drops first, close to the mouth.

choices.text: Evenly across the lake bottom, since still water spreads it out
choices.rationale: Calm water does not spread sand evenly. Sand drops where the current slows, near the mouth; only finer mud is carried farther out.

choices.text: Nowhere, since moving water keeps sand afloat
choices.rationale: Water carries sand only while it moves fast enough. In the calm lake the current slows, and the sand settles.

choices.text: Far out in the middle, since the deepest water pulls it down
choices.rationale: Deep water does not pull sediment toward it. Sand drops as soon as the current slows, which happens where the river meets the lake.

questions.explanation: Moving water can carry sediment only while it has enough energy. When a fast river meets a calm lake, it slows sharply and drops its heaviest grains, the sand, close to the mouth. Finer mud stays suspended longer and settles farther out. Over time these layers can be buried and harden into sedimentary rock.
questions.misconception: Sediment settles evenly wherever water is still, or stays afloat as long as the water moves at all.
questions.hint: What does flowing water need in order to keep carrying sand?

evidence.locator: Section 4. Sedimentary Processes, Physical Sedimentation and Figure 4A
evidence.supports: Physical weathering breaks rock into sediment; wind or water carries it and deposits it when it lacks the energy to keep it moving; breccia (large angular pebbles) and sandstone (small grains, compacted and cemented in layers) form this way.

evidence.title: Delta
evidence.supports: A river slows as it nears its mouth and drops its sediment; heavier, coarser material settles first, and smaller, finer sediment is carried farther.

evidence.title: Sediment and Suspended Sediment (Water Science School)
evidence.supports: Fast-moving water can pick up and move larger particles more easily than slow-moving water; where river water moves too slowly to keep sediment suspended, as in a reservoir, the sediment settles to the bottom.

questions.conditions: The lake water is calm, and the river carries a mix of sand and much finer mud.

questions.prompt: Match each job a geologist needs to do with the tool that fits it best.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Match each of four jobs a geologist needs to do with the tool that fits it best. Jobs: check crystal size on a rock face during a hike; break off a fresh, unweathered piece to study; see the shape of the land and its rock formations across a whole region; and find out which elements a sample contains. Tools: a rock hammer; a lab instrument that measures composition; a hand lens; and a topographic map or remote-sensing image.

left.text: Check crystal size on a rock face during a hike
left.rationale: Hand lens: a small magnifier you can carry, so you can see crystal size right on the rock face.

left.text: Break off a fresh, unweathered piece to study
left.rationale: Rock hammer: it breaks off a piece of rock, exposing a fresh surface that weathering has not changed.

left.text: See the shape of the land and its rock formations across a whole region
left.rationale: Topographic map or remote-sensing image: a topographic map shows the shape of the land, and an image taken from a satellite or airplane shows its surface and rock formations, both across a whole region at once.

left.text: Find out which elements a sample contains
left.rationale: Lab instrument: devices in the lab measure the composition of a rock sample, including which elements it holds.

questions.explanation: Each tool fits a different scale and setting. A hand lens magnifies small details such as crystal size right in the field, and a rock hammer breaks off fresh pieces whose surfaces have not been changed by weathering. Topographic maps and remote-sensing images show a whole region at once, while lab instruments measure what a sample is made of.
questions.misconception: One tool can answer every question about a rock, whatever the scale or setting.
questions.hint: Think about the size of what each job looks at, from tiny crystals to a whole region.

evidence.locator: Section 7. How Scientists Investigate Rocks (text and photo captions, rendered page)
evidence.supports: Tools used to collect and study rocks include rock hammers, hand lenses, microscopes, remote sensing technology, topographic maps and devices that measure composition; a photo shows a scientist inspecting a rock with a magnifying lens; samples go to a lab, where instruments analyze composition, texture and crystal size; scientists map nearby rock formations.

evidence.title: Collecting Rocks
evidence.supports: The geologist's hammer is used to break off fresh rock specimens; the hand lens (pocket magnifier) is used to identify mineral grains, with six- to ten-power magnification best.

evidence.title: Breaking off the weathered surface of lavas in the Clear Lake Volcanic Field to sample the fresh, unaltered cores
evidence.supports: Geologists often break off the weathered surfaces of rocks in the field to get at fresh cores, which makes the original mineralogy easier to see.

evidence.title: What is a topographic map?
evidence.supports: A topographic map uses elevation contour lines to show the shape of Earth's surface.

evidence.title: What is remote sensing and what is it used for?
evidence.supports: Remote sensing detects and monitors the physical characteristics of an area from a distance; cameras on satellites and airplanes take images of large areas of Earth's surface.
